About: An invitational retreat of the OpenMind Research Institute — a Canadian non-profit, fully virtual organization whose roadmap is the Alberta Plan for AI Research. This report distills one talk, “Continual Learning,” topic by topic.

The through-line is Sutton's thesis: the biggest AI advances are still ahead, progress is a marathon, and reinforcement learning — not generative AI — is the path to intelligent agents; the main bottleneck is the lack of effective continual-learning algorithms.

Insight 01 · Minds, and why continual learning

OpenMind & the RL-first Bet on Intelligence

OpenMind Research Institute · Banff Retreat · Sutton's perspective
About OpenMind
  • Canadian non-profit, fully virtual research institute
  • Motto: understand minds well enough to build some — how minds arise from a stream of experience
  • Roadmap: the Alberta Plan for AI Research
  • Objective: do fundamental research and share it openly with the world
Sutton's perspective
  • Super-intelligent agents and augmented humans will bring great benefits to the world
  • The most significant AI advancements are still ahead of us
  • AI development is more of a marathon than a sprint
  • Reinforcement learning (RL) — not generative AI — is the key path to developing intelligent agents
  • The main challenge is the lack of effective learning algorithms
[1] R. Sutton et al., “The Alberta Plan for AI Research,” arXiv:2208.11173, 2022.
Insight 02 · Minds, and why continual learning

What Is a Mind? Goal-seeking, Adaptive, Situated

Continual Learning (talk) · McCarthy · Sutton — ‘reward is enough’
Goal-seeking
  • Intelligence is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals (McCarthy & Sutton)
  • Reward hypothesis: goals & purposes = maximizing the expected cumulative scalar reward
  • Reward-is-enough hypothesis: intelligence and its abilities subserve reward maximization
Adapting behavior
  • Biological minds naturally adapt behavior to goals in complex, dynamic environments
  • Society is comfortable with the adaptive behavior of animals
  • Most ML / engineering systems are fixed and non-adaptive, built on static models of predefined domains
Situated in experience
  • Biological minds adapt within one ongoing, open stream of experience — not independent data inputs
  • Most ML assumes i.i.d. data, making it hard to adapt to real-time, open-world settings
  • Open-world learning needs online learning, incremental updates and real-time adaptability — not captured by current ML theory
[2] D. Silver et al., “Reward is Enough,” Artificial Intelligence, vol. 299, 2021.
Insight 03 · Minds, and why continual learning

Constant vs Continual Learning

Continual Learning (talk) · OpenMind Banff Retreat
The distinction
  • Constant learning: a train phase, then a frozen model used for test
  • Continual learning: the agent stays in the state–action–reward loop and keeps learning past ‘test’
Agents that learn and adapt
  • Learning/adapting agents face non-stationary environments — changing data, policies and value functions
  • Reinforcement learning can handle some degree of non-stationarity naturally
  • Continual learning in open environments is a central challenge for minds
[3] OpenMind Research Institute, “Continual Learning,” Banff Retreat, Oct 2024.
Insight 04 · Agents in a big world

A Common Architecture for Continual RL Agents

Continual Learning (talk) · the Alberta Plan agent model
The four components
  • Perception — produces the state representation used by all other components
  • Reactive policies — quickly produce actions that achieve high reward or features
  • Value functions — evaluate how well things are going and change the policy (learning)
  • Transition model — predict consequences of alternative choices and change the policy (planning)
What each learns, continually
  • Continual supervised representation / feature finding; continual generalized value-function prediction
  • Continual actor-critic control; planning with reward, search control and exploration
Prototype systems
  • One-step model-based RL with continual function approximation
  • STOMP — Stochastic Trajectory Optimization for Motion Planning
  • Intelligence amplification — enhancing human decision-making with AI
[4] OpenMind Research Institute, “Continual Learning — RL Agent Architecture,” Banff Retreat, 2024.
Insight 05 · Agents in a big world

A Little Agent in a Big World

K. Javed & R. Sutton · Big World Hypothesis, 2024
What makes an agent small
  • The agent is constrained relative to the world: an information-capacity limit = the entropy of agent state, in bits
  • Traditional theory: hone in on good actions and refine over time, with vanishing benefit to exploration
  • Small agent, big world ⇒ want more capacity; non-stationary exploration ⇒ acquire info relevant to the future, forget the rest
Decision-aware model learning
  • Model what matters for decisions: Value-Aware (VAML) & Policy-Aware (PAML) model learning, distributional-equivalent variants
  • Much recent work: Predictron, VPN, TreeQN, GAMPS, value-targeted regression, muZero, value-equivalent sampling
  • Continual Knowledge Re-Grounding (KnoReG): benefit from an approximate model, then continually correct it against the real world (OS-VI update)
There is hope
  • There are new ways an approximate model of the world can help a small agent
  • You are not limited to choosing only an inaccurate or only an accurate model
[5] K. Javed & R. Sutton, “The Big World Hypothesis and its Ramifications for AI,” RLC, 2024.
Insight 06 · Agents in a big world

Efficiency vs Generality: Bias, Compute & the Bitter Lesson

R. Sutton — ‘The Bitter Lesson’ · vs the Big World Hypothesis
The trade-off
  • A trade-off between generality and sample efficiency
  • You can improve efficiency by adding bias, at the cost of generality
  • RL defines an extremely general set of problems
Two levers, two conflicts
  • Add bias to the agent — in conflict with the Bitter Lesson and the Big World Hypothesis
  • Use more computation — in conflict with the Big World Hypothesis
The Bitter Lesson
  • Building in knowledge helps short-term and is satisfying, but plateaus and even inhibits progress long-term
  • Breakthroughs eventually arrive from scaling computation via search and learning
Big World Hypothesis
  • The environment is significantly larger and more complex than the agent acting within it
  • As compute grows, environment complexity grows too — the world stays much larger than the agent (Javed & Sutton, 2024)
[6] R. Sutton, “The Bitter Lesson,” incompleteideas.net, 2019.
Insight 07 · From batch to streaming

Batch vs Streaming Learning

M. Elsayed et al. · “Streaming Deep RL Finally Works”, 2024
Streaming vs batch methods
  • Classic streaming — TD(λ), Q(λ), SARSA(λ), AC(λ) — do not work with deep networks
  • Batch — PPO, SAC, DQN, Rainbow — do work with deep networks, but need replay buffers
Why streaming matters
  • Natural intelligence processes experience as a continuous stream — sense, act and learn moment-by-moment
  • Update immediately per sample, without storing it — resource-friendly and privacy-preserving
  • Promise: on-board learning on phones & microcontrollers; micro/nano-second decisions; democratize deep RL to billions of devices
The status quo
  • Batch RL's success is credited to data efficiency: reusing samples and averaging i.i.d. gradients for reliable updates
  • Streaming RL's failure is blamed on sample inefficiency, instability, and hard step-size choice (per-sample gradient outliers)
Overcoming the stream barrier
  • Stability: a step-size-controlling optimizer, reward scaling, observation normalization
  • Trainability: fix the pre-activation distribution with layer norm
  • Sample efficiency: eligibility traces + sparse initialization (Stream-x)
[7] M. Elsayed et al., “Streaming Deep Reinforcement Learning Finally Works,” arXiv:2410.14606, 2024.
Insight 08 · Industry relevance

Where Continual Learning Pays Off

Applications · Continual Learning talk · industry scenarios
Smart home & IoT
  • Adapt to user preferences over time without manual updates
  • Learn and anticipate changing user habits (e.g. a HarmonyOS smart home)
Personalized healthcare
  • Continuously improve diagnosis & treatment recommendations as more patient data arrives
  • Tailor treatments over time from a live stream (e.g. a watch / fit band)
Gaming, finance, agriculture
  • Gaming: adapt difficulty and NPC behavior to player skill
  • Finance: adjust trading and portfolio strategies to evolving markets
  • Agriculture: optimize crop management across changing climate, soil and seasons
Why continual learning here
  • Any system in a dynamic environment benefits from real-time adaptation — no periodic re-training
  • Evolve progressively, avoiding costly full re-training cycles (model drift / degradation)
  • Fits memory- and resource-constrained embedded & IoT devices — incremental, low-resource updates
[8] OpenMind Research Institute, “Continual Learning — Applications,” Banff Retreat, 2024.
Insight 09 · Industry relevance

Challenges & Limitations of Continual Learning

Challenges & limitations · Continual Learning talk
Implementation & data
  • Complexity of implementation — must manage knowledge retention while integrating new information
  • Data management — relies on a continuous data stream, often infeasible (e.g. autonomous vehicles need manual labeled data)
  • Overhead in training time and compute to accommodate ongoing updates and refinements
  • Task & data complexity — as tasks grow, model architecture may need to expand, complicating training and inference
Learning failures
  • Catastrophic forgetting — forgets earlier tasks/classes when trained on new data, especially when data is non-sequential
  • Performance degradation in non-stationary environments where distributions change frequently or unpredictably
  • Risk of overfitting to recent data while failing to generalize across all tasks or classes
  • Real-time adaptation is technically challenging when immediate updates on new data are required
Ecosystem gaps
  • Limited benchmarking & evaluation standards — hard to compare approaches or judge effectiveness
  • No validation for safety-critical systems — run-time learning has no controlled-environment validation; dangerous for autonomous vehicles
[9] OpenMind Research Institute, “Continual Learning — Challenges,” Banff Retreat, 2024.
Conclusions

Synthesis — trends, vision, implications

Trends

  • Growing demand for autonomous, smart systems that learn continually from their environment.
  • A shift toward real-time adaptation — fewer manual interventions and re-training cycles.
  • Edge & IoT push toward lightweight, resource-efficient continual learning on-device.

Vision

  • Adaptive, lifelong-learning systems that evolve without forgetting — like human learning.
  • Resource-efficient, scalable AI that runs well under tight compute and memory budgets.
  • Real-time decision-making and genuine human-AI collaboration from live feedback.

Implications for us

  • Reduced retraining cost and a smaller carbon footprint — cheaper, greener AI.
  • Scalability across devices (IoT, edge) and minimized catastrophic forgetting.
  • A strategic edge for autonomous systems and clear cross-sector market differentiation.
